Freight refers to goods or cargo that are being transported from one place to another, especially in large quantities, and usually for a commercial or business purpose.

Think of it this way: when a company in Mumbai ships hundreds of boxes of manufactured goods to a warehouse in Delhi — those boxes of goods, while they are in transit, are called freight.

Almost any physical goods can be freight — raw materials like steel, coal, or wheat; manufactured products like electronics, furniture, or clothing; industrial equipment; food items in bulk; chemicals; and so on.

The key idea is that it is not personal luggage or a small parcel you send to a friend. Freight typically refers to large, heavy, or bulk shipments that move through organized commercial transportation systems.

The word "freight" as a noun has three closely related but slightly different uses:

1. The goods themselves
This is the most straightforward meaning. The goods being transported are the freight.

"The ship was loaded with freight bound for Europe."
"The truck's freight included 200 crates of bottled water."

Here, "freight" simply means the cargo — the physical stuff being moved.

2. The system or method of transporting those goods
"Freight" can also refer to the entire service or system used to transport goods commercially — not just the goods, but the act or mode of shipping them.

"We sent the machinery by freight."
"The company uses freight to deliver goods to retailers."

Here, saying "by freight" means using a commercial cargo-transport service, as opposed to, say, carrying it yourself or using a courier.

This is why you'll often see terms like:

  • air freight — goods transported by aircraft
  • sea freight / ocean freight — goods transported by ship
  • road freight — goods transported by trucks
  • rail freight — goods transported by train

In each case, "freight" refers to the mode/system of commercial cargo transport.

3. The charge or cost for transporting goods
"Freight" can also mean the fee you pay to have goods transported.

"The freight on this shipment was ₹15,000."
"Who will pay the freight — the buyer or the seller?"

Here, it works just like the word "fare" (what you pay to travel), but for goods instead of passengers. When a business places an order, the question of who pays the freight — the sender or the receiver — is often an important part of the deal.

It helps to understand how "freight" sits alongside related words:

  • Cargo — this is almost a synonym for freight (the goods being transported), but "cargo" is more commonly used for ships and aircraft, while "freight" is broader and also applies to rail and road.
  • Shipment — refers to a specific batch of goods sent at one time. Freight is a more general term; a shipment is one particular instance of it.
  • Goods — just the items themselves, with no implication of movement. Freight implies the goods are specifically in the process of being transported.
  • Logistics — the broader field of planning and managing the movement and storage of goods. Freight is one part of logistics.
Freight in compound words and common phrases

You'll encounter "freight" in many compound words and phrases. Understanding the core meaning makes all of them easy:

  • Freight train — a train that carries goods (cargo), not passengers
  • Freight ship / freighter — a ship designed to carry cargo
  • Freight forwarder — a company or agent that organizes the shipping of goods on behalf of businesses
  • Freight charges — the fees associated with transporting goods
  • Freight terminal — a facility (like a depot or warehouse) where freight is loaded, unloaded, and transferred
  • Dead freight — payment made for cargo space that was reserved but not used
  • Freight in / freight out — accounting terms; "freight in" is the cost of getting goods delivered to your business, "freight out" is the cost of sending goods from your business to customers
A simple way to remember it

Whenever you see the word "freight," ask yourself which of the three things is being talked about:

  1. The stuff being transported (the goods/cargo)
  2. The service of transporting it (shipping by freight)
  3. The cost of transporting it (the freight charge)

In most sentences, the context will make it immediately clear which one applies. And in all three cases, the central idea is always the same: the large-scale, commercial movement of physical goods.
